questions.q: What does an entry in sys_audit actually capture?
options: The field's old value, its new value, who changed it, and when, for a field configured to be audited
A screenshot of the record at the moment it was saved
Only the name of the table where a change occurred, with no field-level detail
The full text of every script that ran during the save, regardless of auditing configuration
questions.explain: sys_audit is the field-level change-history ledger: old value, new value, who, and when, for audited fields.

questions.q: Is auditing automatically on for every field on every table in ServiceNow?
options: No — which tables and fields get audited is a configuration decision, set per field through the Dictionary entry
Yes, every field change on every table is captured in sys_audit by default with no setup required
Only fields on the Incident table are ever audited, by platform design
Auditing is a one-time, instance-wide toggle with no per-field control
questions.explain: Auditing is configured per table and per field. An un-audited field's changes are never written to sys_audit, and that history can't be recovered after the fact.

questions.q: What happens if a field has auditing turned off and it changes repeatedly over time?
options: No sys_audit entry is ever created for those changes, and that change history is not recoverable later
ServiceNow automatically backfills the missing audit entries the next time anyone queries sys_audit
The field's changes are stored in a separate, hidden table that can be enabled retroactively
The record itself becomes read-only until auditing is turned back on
questions.explain: If auditing wasn't on when the changes happened, there is no sys_audit record of them — the history was simply never captured.

questions.q: What real, honest tradeoff does this lesson describe for turning on auditing for every field on every table?
options: It creates real storage growth and additional write overhead on every save, for change history that mostly never gets reviewed
It has no real cost at all, since sys_audit entries take up no measurable storage
It actually makes the instance faster by reducing the number of fields developers need to maintain
It is required by ServiceNow licensing and cannot be configured any other way
questions.explain: Every additional audited field adds a sys_audit write on every update to it, across every record — real overhead that compounds at scale, often for history nobody reviews.

questions.q: What is the practical, defensible approach to deciding which fields to audit?
options: Audit specific sensitive or compliance-relevant fields deliberately, rather than defaulting to auditing everything or auditing nothing
Audit only fields that are never expected to change, since those are easiest to track
Audit every field for exactly 30 days and then disable auditing platform-wide
Never audit anything, since all auditing is prohibitively expensive at any scale
questions.explain: Selective auditing — chosen around whether someone would genuinely need a change history for a given field — is the realistic middle ground between auditing nothing and auditing everything.
